body.heading: Crosswords meet arithmetic
paragraphs: A Kakuro grid looks like a crossword: black cells carry clues, white cells wait to be filled. Each clue is a sum, pointing across or down, and you fill the white cells with digits 1 to 9 that add up to it. The golden rule: within a single sum, no digit may repeat.
The name is shortened from the Japanese “kasan kurosu” — addition cross. Kakuro has been a newspaper staple in Japan for decades and a quiet favourite everywhere else ever since.

body.heading: The magic of unique sums
paragraphs: Some sums have only one possible combination, and finding them is the key that opens the puzzle. A sum of 3 across two cells must be 1 + 2. A sum of 4 in two cells must be 1 + 3 (2 + 2 is banned by the no-repeat rule). At the top end, 16 in two cells is 7 + 9, and 17 is 8 + 9.
Three-cell sums have their own certainties: 7 in three cells can only be 1 + 2 + 4. Learn these “magic blocks” and a Kakuro grid starts offering you free cells in the first minute.

body.heading: Try it: build the reflex
paragraphs: Practise by listing combinations: how many ways can two different digits make 10? (1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 — four ways.) Which two-digit sums have exactly one way? Working this out once teaches you more than solving three puzzles by luck.
When you solve, begin where two restricted sums cross — a cell belonging to a “3 in two” across and a “17 in two” down has very few places to hide. Intersections are where Kakuro confesses.

takeaway: Kakuro is arithmetic with a crossword's skeleton: learn the sums that have only one combination and the grid begins to open.
